items.title: Carmen Leggio interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998
items.q: When I came back I was a white man fronting a black group, Keter, Louis Derry and June Bug.

ctx.x: This club in Washington where you had these 17 weeks, you had a racially mixed band, was it any problem with that?

When I was with Bill Potts, it was a white group. When I came back I was a white man fronting a black group, Keter, Louis Derry and June Bug. And still whites wouldn’t dare come up. And at that time still the blacks couldn’t — how do I put it — they were stopped from doing things that were supposed to be done. But by seeing the way we played, and what was going on, and people looking at us and seeing how we got along, before you know it the whites were seeping in and we started getting an interracial crowd,…
The music has always had a bit part of breaking that down.

items.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996
items.q: And the lady said, “if you can get a group together I’d like for you to come in.” So he brought a drummer from Tarrytown, and a piano player from New Rochelle and myself.

ctx.x: It didn’t take you too long before you started playing out.

I was going out a year later. The next year I went down to Washington. A saxophone player from White Plains, Carmen Leggio, had been stationed down there in the service. And when he got out he used to go jam at this club. And the lady said, “if you can get a group together I’d like for you to come in.” So he brought a drummer from Tarrytown, and a piano player from New Rochelle and myself. And we came down there, you know, green. First time away from home, we got out and the whole bit. And we came in for four…

saxophone player named Rick Henderson called me in December to see if I could come down and do a month with him in January at a club down there, sort of like a supper club, and then Bostic came to town and heard me and asked me did I want to go with him, and that’s how it went on.
